lead: A named polymer is a fact sheet: monomer, repeat unit, growth type, use. Addition polymers use one alkene monomer and lose nothing. Condensation polymers usually use two bifunctional monomers and lose one small molecule such as water or HCl per new bond. Nylon 6 is the exception: caprolactam rings open and join head to tail, losing nothing, so its repeat unit has the same mass as caprolactam, 113 g/mol. PVC pipes, PET bottles and tyre rubber are familiar families.
prereq: You need: 5.1 for repeat units and 5.3 for chain growth versus step growth.

blocks.text: Addition polymers start from one C=C monomer. Chain growth adds units with no atom loss, so the repeat unit has the same atoms as the monomer. Each row reads monomer → repeat unit → use.

Three entries deserve a second look. PTFE has four fluorine atoms on the double-bonded carbons, making it inert and slippery. PP and high-density PE usually use Ziegler-Natta catalysts (5.4); chain regularity then decides stiffness (5.5).

Condensation polymers usually form by step growth between two bifunctional monomers; each new bond releases one small molecule, usually water or HCl. Subtract it once per bond. Nylon 6 is the exception.

items: Nylon 6,6: adipic acid + hexamethylenediamine; two water molecules leave per repeat unit. Ropes, tyre cords.
Nylon 6: caprolactam rings open and join head to tail; nothing is lost, so –NH–(CH₂)₅–CO– has the same formula and mass as caprolactam, 113 g/mol.
PET: ethylene glycol + terephthalic acid; two water molecules leave per repeat unit. Bottles, polyester fibre.
Polycarbonate: bisphenol A + phosgene; two HCl molecules leave per repeat unit. Helmets, large water jars.
Bakelite: phenol + methanal; cross-linked. Switch boards, pan handles.

blocks.text: Bakelite and urea-formaldehyde are thermosets: cross-links lock chains into a network, so they char instead of melting. PET, nylon and polycarbonate are thermoplastics and can be remelted.

Natural rubber is cis-polyisoprene (isoprene, C₅H₈); cis double bonds make chains coil and snap back. Vulcanisation heats raw rubber with sulfur, forming bridges. About 2–3% sulfur gives flexible tyre rubber; about 30% gives hard ebonite. SBR (styrene-butadiene rubber) is the largest-volume synthetic rubber, with butadiene rubber and natural rubber close behind; it is the main tyre tread. Nitrile rubber, butadiene plus acrylonitrile, is a specialty grade for oil-resistant fuel hoses.

Silicones (polysiloxanes) have an Si–O–Si backbone with methyl groups. Strong Si–O bonds give heat stability; the flexible backbone gives oiliness. Uses: lubricating oils and water-repelling sealants for tiles and glass.

figure.caption: The tree groups six must-know polymers into addition and condensation families, with a monomer or use as reminder. Every member of the condensation branch shown loses a small molecule while built.

examples.question: Nylon 6,6: adipic acid (146 g/mol) + hexamethylenediamine (116 g/mol); two water molecules (18 g/mol each) leave per repeat unit. Find repeat-unit mass and mass at DP = 100.
examples.check:
adipic = 146
diamine = 116
water = 18
repeat_unit = adipic + diamine - 2 * water
print(repeat_unit)
print(repeat_unit * 100)

examples.question: PET: ethylene glycol (62 g/mol) + terephthalic acid (166 g/mol); two water molecules leave per repeat unit. Find repeat-unit mass.

traps: Never use monomer mass for a chain calculation. Subtract the small molecule per repeat unit, twice for nylon 6,6 and PET, not at all for nylon 6.
Nylon 6,6 has two different six-carbon monomers; nylon 6 has one monomer, caprolactam.
Vulcanisation is sulfur cross-linking, not polymerisation; sulfur percentage decides soft rubber versus ebonite.
PVC repeat unit is –CH₂–CHCl–, not poly(vinyl alcohol).
Addition polymers lose no atoms, so repeat-unit mass equals monomer mass.

quiz.q: Name PVC's monomer and one use.
quiz.a: Vinyl chloride, CH₂=CHCl; pipes and cable insulation.

quiz.q: Why is PET's repeat unit lighter than its monomer sum?
quiz.a: Each ester bond loses one water; two per repeat unit, so subtract 2 × 18 = 36 g/mol.

quiz.q: Ethylene glycol 62 g/mol and terephthalic acid 166 g/mol; find PET repeat-unit mass.
Why does vulcanised rubber not flow on heating while polythene does?
quiz.a: Sulfur cross-links make a network; polythene chains are separate and slide.

quiz.q: Why use nitrile rubber for a fuel hose, not SBR?
quiz.a: Acrylonitrile units are polar, so petrol does not swell it; SBR is a hydrocarbon and swells.

quiz.q: Why can PET be remelted but Bakelite cannot?
quiz.a: PET is thermoplastic; Bakelite is cross-linked and chars.

beyond: Not for exam. Industry sorts by tonnage: PE, PP and PVC dominate plastics; SBR leads synthetic rubbers, with butadiene and natural rubber close behind. Recycling uses resin codes because mixed plastics cannot melt into one useful material. Newer work uses bio-based diacids for PET and peroxide or radiation cross-linking. Search: thermoplastic elastomers, bio-based polyesters, recycling codes.
